Tile
TYL
n. (a flat clay brick used for building or for drawing upon; Ezekiel's map of a besieged city)
Old English tigele, from Latin tegula, from tegere, to cover. In Ezekiel it renders Hebrew lebenah, a brick — the same word used of the bricks Israel made in Egypt.

Biblical Definition

Thou also, son of man, take thee a tile, and lay it before thee, and pourtray upon it the city, even Jerusalem. Ezekiel is told to draw a map on a clay brick — the ordinary building material of Babylon, where he was in exile — and then to besiege it: lay siege against it, build a fort, cast a mount, set the camp, set battering rams round about. A grown prophet playing with a brick in the street, in front of people who had lost that city, acting out what was about to happen to what was left of it. Ezekiel's ministry is full of these enacted signs because words had stopped landing. The other tiles in Scripture are a roof. When four men could not get their paralysed friend to Jesus through the crowd, they went upon the housetop, and let him down through the tiling with his couch into the midst before Jesus; Mark says plainly that they uncovered the roof and broke it up. They wrecked somebody's house to get a man to Christ, and the Lord, seeing their faith, forgave his sins and healed him without a word about the roof. One tile bears a siege, the other bears a hole; both were clay in the hands of men who believed God meant what he said.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a plate or piece of baked clay used for covering the roofs of buildings; a thin plate of baked clay.

expand to see more

TILE, n. A plate or piece of baked clay used for covering the roofs of buildings.

TILING, n. A roof covered with tiles; tiles in general.

BRICK, n. A mass of earth, chiefly clay, first moistened and made fine by working, then formed into a long square and baked.

PORTRAY, v.t. To paint or draw the likeness of anything in colors; to describe in words.

SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender.

Key Scripture

Ezekiel 4:1 — "Thou also, son of man, take thee a tile, and lay it before thee, and pourtray upon it the city, even Jerusalem:"

Ezekiel 4:2 — "And lay siege against it, and build a fort against it, and cast a mount against it; set the camp also against it, and set battering rams against it round about."

Luke 5:19 — "And when they could not find by what way they might bring him in because of the multitude, they went upon the housetop, and let him down through the tiling with his couch into the midst before Jesus."

Mark 2:4 — "And when they could not come nigh unto him for the press, they uncovered the roof where he was: and when they had broken it up, they let down the bed wherein the sick of the palsy lay."

Modern Corruption

Dramatized preaching is mistaken for Ezekiel's sign-acts, and persistence in bringing people to Christ is mistaken for pressure; both scenes were obedience under cost, ordered or rewarded by God himself.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Ezekiel's brick was commanded, not invented. He did not devise a memorable illustration to hold an audience; God told him to take the tile, and then told him to lie on his side for three hundred and ninety days, and to eat bread baked in a measured way. The sign-acts are prophecy in another medium, given by the Lord to a prophet whose people would not hear words. A preacher who stages a spectacle of his own choosing is doing the opposite of what Ezekiel did, however similar it looks from the back of the room.

The four men who broke up a roof teach the other half. They had one aim, they met a real obstacle, and they went through the obstacle rather than home. Mark notes what Jesus saw: when Jesus saw their faith — theirs, the carriers', not only the sick man's. There is such a thing as pressing a person toward Christ in a way that is merely pressure, and Scripture has no interest in that. But there is also a quiet unbelief that calls its own passivity respect. These men dug through clay tiles over somebody else's head, and the Lord commended them for it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew lebenah (H3843), a brick or tile; matsor (H4692), a siege; Greek keramos (G2766), a roof tile; apostegazo (G648), to unroof.

expand to see more

Hebrew lebenah (H3843) — a brick; the same word as the bricks of Egyptian bondage, now a map of Jerusalem.

Hebrew matsor (H4692) — siege, entrenchment; what Ezekiel was told to build against his own clay city.

Greek keramos (G2766) — a roof tile, potter's clay; the tiling Luke says they let him through.

Greek apostegazo (G648) — to unroof, to take off the covering; Mark's blunt verb for what they did.

Hebrew oth (H226) — a sign; Ezekiel is told the whole performance is a sign to the house of Israel.

Usage

"“take thee a tile... and pourtray upon it the city” — prophecy drawn on a brick."

"“let him down through the tiling” — a roof opened to reach Christ."

"“when they had broken it up” — Mark's account of the cost."
